latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent upstream drive from infection, obstetric tissue factor release, trauma, malignancy, acute leukemia, severe inflammation, heat injury, or other triggers. The trigger is not part of the disease name; it modulates the DIC landscape by sustaining tissue-factor and endothelial-injury signals.
Systemic activation of the extrinsic coagulation pathway with excess thrombin generation, fibrin formation, and loss of localization of coagulation.
Fibrin-rich thrombi form in small vessels and sometimes larger vessels, producing renal cortical, pulmonary, CNS, myocardial, skin, limb, and mesenteric ischemia.

Platelets, fibrinogen, and soluble clotting factors are consumed faster than they are replenished, causing thrombocytopenia, PT/INR prolongation, aPTT prolongation, hypofibrinogenemia in decompensated disease, and bleeding.

Plasmin generation degrades cross-linked fibrin and fibrinogen, raising D-dimer and fibrin degradation products. Hyperfibrinolytic phenotypes bleed severely; sepsis-dominant phenotypes can have relatively suppressed fibrinolysis but still high D-dimer.
Antithrombin and protein C pathways are consumed, degraded, or insufficiently synthesized, amplifying thrombin generation and predisposing to purpura fulminans, limb ischemia, and organ thrombosis.

Cytokines, complement, neutrophil extracellular traps, hypoxia, and endothelial glycocalyx injury expose procoagulant surfaces, increase permeability, impair anticoagulant signaling, and couple DIC to shock and organ failure.

Hepatic acute-phase fibrinogen synthesis can mask consumption, especially in sepsis or inflammatory malignancy, so fibrinogen may be normal or high early and fall only when consumption exceeds synthesis.

Reduced platelets, depleted fibrinogen and factors, and fibrinolysis produce oozing from lines, mucosal bleeding, hematuria, hemoptysis, obstetric hemorrhage, GI bleeding, pulmonary hemorrhage, and intracranial hemorrhage.
Microthrombi, shock, hypoxia, and bleeding converge into AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, ischemic stroke, myocardial injury, hepatic injury, skin necrosis, and multi-organ failure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Diverse triggers converge on tissue-factor exposure or expression and thrombin generation.
Persistent trigger maintains endothelial activation, cytokine signaling, complement activation, hypoxia, or direct vascular injury.
Uncontrolled source, placenta/tissue factor exposure, untreated malignancy, or unresolved trauma keeps trigger-control adequacy low.
Excess thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, causing intravascular fibrin deposition and microvascular occlusion.
Sustained clot formation consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and coagulation factors.
Cross-linked fibrin triggers plasmin-mediated breakdown with D-dimer and FDP generation.
Thrombin generation and endothelial injury consume or downregulate antithrombin, protein C, and thrombomodulin pathways.
Endothelial activation exposes procoagulant surfaces and amplifies tissue-factor signaling.
Inflammatory cytokines increase hepatic fibrinogen synthesis, which can keep fibrinogen normal or high despite consumption.
Platelets are incorporated into thrombi and consumed in systemic coagulation activation.
Consumption of extrinsic and common pathway factors prolongs PT and raises INR.
Consumption of intrinsic and common pathway factors prolongs aPTT when decompensated.
Fibrinogen is consumed into fibrin clots and can fall profoundly in obstetric, APL-associated, traumatic, or late decompensated DIC.
Acute-phase synthesis explains normal or high fibrinogen in some sepsis-dominant DIC despite other DIC markers.

Many DIC presentations are driven by infection, severe inflammation, malignancy, obstetric catastrophe, trauma, or heat injury; fever tracks the upstream trigger rather than being a DIC-specific coagulation sign.
Inflammatory triggers and endothelial injury commonly raise CRP in DIC, especially sepsis-associated, malignant, obstetric, traumatic, and heat-injury phenotypes.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: mainly when the DIC trigger is bacterial infection or septic shock; low/normal values do not exclude noninfectious DIC
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacterial sepsis is a common DIC trigger and can produce high procalcitonin alongside the coagulation phenotype.
Breakdown of cross-linked fibrin generates D-dimer, often markedly elevated.
Fibrin and fibrinogen degradation products rise with plasmin activity.
Antithrombin is consumed, degraded, lost through capillary leak, or underproduced during severe DIC.
Protein C pathway impairment is prominent in purpura fulminans and thrombotic DIC phenotypes.
Fibrin microthrombi impair tissue perfusion and oxygen extraction across organs.
Low platelets, depleted fibrinogen, and factor depletion produce bleeding.
Fibrinolytic degradation destabilizes hemostatic clots and amplifies bleeding.
DIC bleeding appears as line oozing, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding, hematuria, hemoptysis, obstetric bleeding, GI bleeding, or CNS bleeding.
Clinically significant bleeding lowers hemoglobin, with dilution from resuscitation sometimes contributing.
Consumptive and fibrinolytic coagulopathy raises the daily hazard of major bleeding.
Microvascular fibrin and thrombin generation can extend to venous, arterial, limb, or organ thrombotic events.
Protein C pathway failure and dermal microvascular thrombosis produce purpura fulminans.
Renal hypoperfusion and renal microthrombi produce AKI.
Shock and microvascular oxygen extraction failure raise lactate.
Bleeding, vasoplegia, capillary leak, myocardial injury, and shock physiology lower perfusion pressure.
ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, embolic thrombosis, or shock-related lung injury lower oxygenation.
Shock encephalopathy, CNS ischemia, intracranial hemorrhage, or metabolic organ failure can cause altered mental status.
DIC microthrombi and shock raise the event hazard of AKI.
Endothelial injury, capillary leak, microthrombi, and transfusion burden raise ARDS hazard.
Persistent DIC with organ failure, bleeding, or thrombosis is a high short-term mortality state.

axes.shape_free_text: Falls dynamically from baseline; overt DIC often <100, severe consumption <50, but early sepsis DIC can start near normal before rapid decline.
PT/INR prolongation is central to DIC and helps distinguish DIC from TTP/CAPS-like TMA where PT is often normal.
aPTT may be mildly to markedly prolonged as intrinsic/common pathway factors are consumed; can be near-normal early.

Bidirectional DIC axis: low in decompensated, obstetric, traumatic, APL-like or hyperfibrinolytic DIC; normal/high in inflammatory sepsis-dominant DIC when acute-phase synthesis temporarily offsets consumption.
Usually markedly elevated, often >5 ug/mL FEU and sometimes >30-80 in fulminant DIC; also elevated in thrombosis, sepsis, malignancy, pregnancy, and inflammation.
FDP rises with fibrin and fibrinogen breakdown; useful where reported instead of or alongside D-dimer.
Often reduced in sepsis-associated and severe DIC; low values mark loss of natural anticoagulant buffering and thrombotic/organ-failure risk.
Can fall in severe DIC, especially purpura fulminans and septic shock phenotypes; congenital or acquired baseline deficiency amplifies skin necrosis risk.
Falls with major bleeding, hemodilution, and sometimes microangiopathic fragmentation; isolated severe MAHA with normal PT/aPTT favors TTP over DIC.

May be present from fibrin strands and microangiopathy, but usually less dominant than TTP; very high schistocytes plus severe ADAMTS13 deficiency and normal coagulation tests points away from isolated DIC.
Rises with tissue ischemia, shock liver, hemolysis, malignancy, or organ infarction; not specific for DIC.
Rises with AKI from shock, renal microthrombi, cortical necrosis, rhabdomyolysis, or underlying trigger.
Rises with shock, microvascular ischemia, severe bleeding, or impaired hepatic clearance.
Fever or chills from the upstream DIC trigger; common in sepsis-associated, inflammatory, malignant, heat-injury, and transfusion-related contexts but not specific for DIC.
Inflammatory burden of the upstream DIC trigger and thromboinflammation; often high in sepsis-associated or inflammatory DIC and less informative in isolated consumptive coagulopathy.

Bacterial infection trigger intensity in infection-associated DIC; may be very high in septic DIC but should remain low in obstetric, traumatic, malignant, or APL-like DIC unless bacterial infection coexists.
May fall from hemorrhage, septic/vasoplegic trigger, cardiomyopathy, capillary leak, or multi-organ failure.
Can fall with ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, shock, or transfusion-related lung injury.
Rises with shock liver, ischemic tissue injury, hemolysis, or underlying trigger.
Rises with hepatic ischemia, hepatic trigger, or multi-organ failure.
Can rise with myocardial microthrombi, demand ischemia, PE, shock, or myocarditis-like trigger; high values signal mortality risk but are not DIC-specific.
Delirium, reduced GCS, seizure, syncope, coma, or focal CNS signs from shock, intracranial hemorrhage, CNS ischemia, or metabolic organ failure.
Composite visible bleeding burden: line oozing, ecchymosis, mucosal bleeding, vaginal bleeding, hematuria, hemoptysis, GI bleeding, pulmonary hemorrhage, surgical bleeding, or CNS bleeding.
Petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, or non-blanching hemorrhagic lesions from thrombocytopenia and dermal microvascular injury.
Microscopic or gross urinary tract bleeding from coagulopathy or renal/urothelial injury.
Blood-streaked sputum to pulmonary hemorrhage; can reflect DIC bleeding, PE, infection, vasculitis, or malignancy context.
Rapidly progressive purpura with dermal thrombosis, hemorrhagic necrosis, and high limb loss risk; occurs in severe DIC with protein C pathway failure, not only meningococcemia.
Cold, cyanotic, mottled, painful, or gangrenous digits/limbs from microvascular thrombosis, vasopressors, shock, or purpura fulminans.
Extent of dermal/full-thickness skin necrosis attributable to DIC microvascular thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction.
Daily hazard of clinically important bleeding requiring transfusion, procedure, ICU support, or causing organ compromise.
Hazard of intracranial hemorrhage, especially with severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, anticoagulation, APL-like phenotype, trauma, obstetric catastrophe, or CNS lesion.
Hazard of diffuse alveolar or pulmonary bleeding in severe coagulopathy, lung injury, malignancy, infection, or vasculitic mimic context.
Hazard of overt GI bleeding or stress-ulcer bleeding amplified by DIC coagulopathy.
Hazard of venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, arterial thrombosis, limb ischemia, organ infarction, or microvascular thrombotic progression.
Hazard of AKI from shock, renal microthrombi, cortical necrosis, hemoglobinuria, or trigger disease.
Hazard of ARDS from endothelial injury, capillary leak, microthrombi, sepsis/trauma context, aspiration, pulmonary hemorrhage, or transfusion-related lung injury.
Hazard of myocardial microthrombosis, demand ischemia, PE strain, arrhythmia, or shock cardiomyopathy during DIC.
Hazard of CNS ischemic thrombosis in thrombotic DIC phenotypes; must be separated from intracranial hemorrhage hazard.
Hazard of intubation/mechanical ventilation due to ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, shock encephalopathy, or airway protection needs.

Context axis: 1 means the upstream DIC trigger has been removed or controlled; 0 means ongoing uncontrolled infection/source, retained placenta/abruption, active bleeding tissue factor release, untreated malignancy/APL, trauma, or other driver.
Context axis used for treatment gating: current major bleeding, high-risk procedure, postpartum/operative bleeding, CNS/pulmonary/GI hemorrhage, or uncontrolled line oozing.

Context axis: DIC phenotype dominated by thrombosis, acral ischemia, purpura fulminans, PE/DVT, organ infarction, or chronic malignancy-associated clotting rather than active life-threatening bleeding.

Treatment-context axis capturing current or imminent severe bleeding risk from CNS bleed, pulmonary/GI/obstetric bleeding, very low fibrinogen, very low platelets, recent surgery, or invasive procedures.
Risk that plasma-heavy resuscitation worsens pulmonary edema, ARDS, heart failure, renal failure, or transfusion-associated circulatory overload.

Lifespan outcome hazard for D-DIC. High when trigger remains uncontrolled, bleeding is catastrophic, thrombosis causes organ ischemia, or AKI/ARDS/CNS/myocardial failure accumulates. Not a separate death manifold.

axis_couplings.conditionality: strongest when platelet_count below 50 x10^9/L or falling rapidly
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Lower platelets raise major bleeding risk, especially with low fibrinogen or procedures.
Low fibrinogen destabilizes clot formation and is central in obstetric, traumatic, APL-like, and hyperfibrinolytic DIC bleeding.

axis_couplings.conditionality: both prolong when soluble coagulation factor consumption is decompensated
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: PT and aPTT often move together as common pathway factor depletion worsens.
Both reflect fibrin breakdown and usually rise together.

axis_couplings.conditionality: inverse relation can be masked by acute-phase fibrinogen synthesis in sepsis/inflammation
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fibrin formation/breakdown consumes fibrinogen while raising D-dimer, but inflammatory synthesis can keep fibrinogen normal or high.
Observed active bleeding marks a high near-term probability of transfusion-requiring or organ-threatening bleeding.

axis_couplings.conditionality: amplified by severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, anticoagulation, CNS lesion, trauma, or APL-like phenotype
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Global bleeding hazard can transition into ICH, the highest-lethality bleeding event.
Coagulopathy can manifest as hemoptysis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, especially with lung injury.
Renal microthrombi, cortical necrosis, PE/shock, and systemic hypoperfusion raise AKI hazard.
Coronary microthrombi, PE strain, demand ischemia, and shock raise myocardial injury hazard.
Purpura fulminans can progress quickly to full-thickness hemorrhagic skin necrosis.
Falling perfusion pressure increases lactate through tissue hypoxia and impaired clearance.
Hypoxemia indicates worsening lung injury and raises ARDS-related respiratory failure hazard.
AKI in DIC reflects severe microvascular injury and worsens short-term survival.
ARDS and respiratory failure are major mortality pathways in DIC-trigger syndromes.
ICH is one of the highest-lethality DIC complications.
DIC rarely resolves sustainably without controlling the upstream trigger; low adequacy prolongs coagulopathy and organ failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: If the trigger is already removed or controlled, additional causal-control effect on DIC is smaller.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls the upstream driver: antibiotics/source control, uterine evacuation or delivery when obstetric tissue factor source persists, trauma control, malignancy/APL-directed therapy, or withdrawal of offending trigger.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Platelet support is most useful when bleeding or an urgent invasive procedure is present.
When thrombosis dominates and bleeding is absent, platelet transfusion can fuel microthrombosis and is not a causal DIC treatment.

side_effects.interpretation: May worsen thrombotic-predominant DIC if used without bleeding/procedure need.
Transfusion volume can worsen overload in renal or cardiac dysfunction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporarily raises platelet count for active bleeding or procedures while the DIC trigger is being controlled.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Plasma replacement is most useful when factor depletion is causing bleeding or an invasive procedure is unavoidable.
Large-volume plasma can worsen pulmonary edema, ARDS, renal failure, or heart failure.

side_effects.interpretation: Plasma volume can precipitate TACO or worsen respiratory failure.
Transfusion-related lung injury or volume overload can worsen oxygenation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Replaces consumed soluble coagulation factors when bleeding or procedure risk makes PT/aPTT correction clinically relevant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fibrinogen replacement is most consequential in active bleeding or anticipated procedure.
When fibrinogen is not low and thrombosis dominates, extra fibrinogen has less benefit and may increase clot substrate.

side_effects.interpretation: Excess fibrinogen substrate may contribute to thrombosis in thrombotic-predominant states.

treatments.context_specific_role: Corrects low fibrinogen, especially in obstetric, traumatic, APL-like, or hyperfibrinolytic bleeding phenotypes.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transfusion remains usable but must be balanced against overload risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Blood product volume can worsen overload.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports oxygen delivery during bleeding anemia but does not by itself stop DIC.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Heparin is most coherent when thrombosis, acral ischemia, PE/DVT, or chronic malignancy-associated DIC dominates.
Active major bleeding or very low fibrinogen/platelets can make anticoagulation unsafe.

side_effects.interpretation: Anticoagulation can convert compensated coagulopathy into bleeding.
ICH hazard rises when anticoagulation is used in severe coagulopathy or CNS vulnerability.

treatments.context_specific_role: Suppresses thrombin propagation in thrombotic-predominant or chronic DIC phenotypes after bleeding risk is made acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antifibrinolysis is only coherent when bleeding is driven by excessive fibrinolysis after factor/fibrinogen support.
Blocking fibrinolysis in thrombotic DIC can worsen microvascular thrombosis.

side_effects.interpretation: Can worsen pathologic clot persistence if thrombin generation is not controlled.

treatments.context_specific_role: Selected use for life-threatening hyperfibrinolytic bleeding; not a general DIC therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vasopressors cannot restore durable perfusion if hemorrhage remains uncontrolled.

side_effects.interpretation: High-dose vasopressors can worsen acral ischemia in purpura fulminans/shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Maintains perfusion during shock while causal and hemostatic treatment takes effect.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Circuit anticoagulation must be adapted when bleeding risk is high.

side_effects.interpretation: Dialysis catheter placement and circuit anticoagulation can add bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports severe AKI, refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload during DIC-related organ failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ventilation supports oxygenation but cannot stop ongoing pulmonary hemorrhage.

side_effects.interpretation: Intubation and lines can bleed in severe coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supports oxygenation and lung mechanics during ARDS, pulmonary hemorrhage, or shock-related respiratory failure.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises tissue-factor/thromboinflammatory drive; fibrinogen may be normal or high early from acute-phase response.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Inflammatory fibrinogen synthesis can mask consumption.
Sepsis-associated fibrin turnover and microthrombi markedly raise D-dimer.
Septic and inflammatory DIC triggers raise acute-phase inflammatory markers.
Bacterial infection or septic shock trigger can produce high procalcitonin in infection-associated DIC.
Infectious DIC triggers commonly present with fever or chills.

placental_abruption_amniotic_fluid_embol.trajectory_modulation: Rapid hyperfibrinolytic/consumptive DIC with very low fibrinogen, abrupt bleeding, and need for source removal or uterine control.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Obstetric DIC can deplete fibrinogen earlier and more profoundly than many other triggers.
Obstetric bleeding and DIC amplify each other.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can produce chronic compensated DIC with recurrent thrombosis and high D-dimer, then convert to acute bleeding DIC when consumption outpaces synthesis.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Cancer-associated tissue factor, mucins, and inflammatory procoagulants increase venous/arterial thrombosis.

present.trajectory_modulation: APL and some acute leukemias strongly drive DIC; peripheral blasts/promyelocytes and marrow findings belong in context/confirmatory evidence for the trigger, not in the DIC disease name.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: APL-like hyperfibrinolysis commonly produces low fibrinogen.
APL-associated DIC has high early catastrophic bleeding risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Massive tissue factor release and endothelial injury produce early coagulopathy with mixed bleeding, thrombosis, shock, and hypofibrinogenemia.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Shock and tissue injury amplify lactate.
Trauma/necrosis DIC commonly coexists with surgical bleeding.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can mimic DIC with high INR, low fibrinogen, and thrombocytopenia while also reducing reserve to compensate true DIC.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Baseline hepatic synthetic failure raises INR independent of acute DIC.
Portal hypertension and marrow suppression can lower platelets before DIC.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not define DIC but amplifies bleeding and confounds PT/aPTT interpretation depending on the agent.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding at any given platelet/fibrinogen state.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Existing anticoagulation changes safety and dosing of additional heparin.

present.trajectory_modulation: Lowers platelet reserve, making DIC appear more bleeding-prone and reducing specificity of platelet count alone.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Platelet count must be interpreted against baseline marrow/immune/liver context.
Low platelet reserve increases bleeding for a given degree of DIC.

coagulation_tests_normal_with_maha_domin.trajectory_modulation: Severe MAHA/schistocytes, profound thrombocytopenia, neurologic/renal findings, and normal PT/aPTT/fibrinogen favor TTP/HUS/CAPS-like TMA rather than isolated DIC.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Normal PT/INR weakens DIC when TMA evidence dominates.
Normal aPTT weakens DIC when TMA evidence dominates.

present.trajectory_modulation: HLH/MAS can cause coagulopathy and hypofibrinogenemia and may overlap with DIC; very high ferritin, cytopenias, splenomegaly, and hemophagocytic context should remain separate evidence for HLH/MAS.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: HLH/MAS can lower fibrinogen through inflammatory consumption and fibrinolysis.

supportive_care: Serial platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer/FDP, hemoglobin, creatinine, lactate, liver enzymes, and bleeding/thrombosis exam every 4-12 hours during unstable DIC.

Identify and control the upstream trigger: cultures and antimicrobials/source control when infection is suspected, obstetric evacuation/delivery when placental or uterine source persists, trauma/surgical control, and hematology/oncology evaluation for malignancy or APL-like triggers.

Keep confirmatory trigger evidence such as culture speciation, PML-RARA, marrow pathology, placental pathology, antiphospholipid antibodies, or ADAMTS13 in context/confirmatory channels rather than ordinary DIC observations.
Use blood products as temporary hemostatic support while trigger control is underway; reassess after each transfusion because consumption can rapidly recur.
For active bleeding or urgent procedures, monitor fibrinogen closely and replace with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate when low or falling.

Avoid routine platelet transfusion in thrombotic-predominant DIC without bleeding or procedure need; use it when active bleeding, very low platelets, or invasive procedures make platelet support necessary.
Separate bleeding-predominant and thrombotic-predominant phenotypes before anticoagulation; heparin requires active reassessment of platelets, fibrinogen, bleeding, renal function, and HIT risk.

Monitor for organ ischemia: urine output and creatinine for AKI, oxygenation and chest imaging for ARDS/pulmonary hemorrhage, ECG/troponin for myocardial injury, neurologic checks and head imaging if mental status changes.
Use low-volume fibrinogen concentrate instead of plasma-heavy replacement when volume overload risk is high and the clinical setting permits.

Prevent iatrogenic bleeding: compressible-line sites when possible, ultrasound guidance for central access, avoid unnecessary arterial punctures, and correct fibrinogen/platelets before unavoidable procedures.
Coordinate hematology, ICU, transfusion medicine, and the trigger-specific team (infectious diseases, obstetrics, trauma surgery, oncology, or source-control service).
After stabilization, review the case for hidden trigger and mimic disease: APL/acute leukemia, TTP/HUS/CAPS, HLH/MAS, liver failure, anticoagulant effect, and advanced malignancy.
